text: Le Rêve (The Dream) is a 1932 oil on canvas painting (130 × 97 cm) by Pablo Picasso, then 50 years old, depicting his 22-year-old mistress Marie-Thérèse Walter. It was said to have been painted in one afternoon on 24 January 1932 and belongs to Picasso's period of distorted depictions, characterized by oversimplified outlines and contrasted colors reminiscent of early cubism. Critics have noted the painting's erotic content, specifically an erect penis in the upturned face of the model, which is believed to symbolize Picasso's own. Purchased for $7,000 in 1941 by Victor and Sally Ganz of New York City, the painting became part of their 50-year collection of works by only five artists: Picasso, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg, Frank Stella, and Eva Hesse. After the Ganzes died—Victor in 1987 and Sally in 1997—their collection, including Le Rêve, was sold at Christie's on 11 November 1997 to settle inheritance tax, with Le Rêve fetching an unexpectedly high $48.4 million, at the time the fourth most expensive painting sold (tenth when adjusted for inflation). The entire collection brought $206.5 million, while the Ganzes had spent approximately $2 million over their lifetime collecting these works. The 1997 buyer of Le Rêve was Wolfgang Flöttl, an Austrian-born investment fund manager who also briefly owned Van Gogh's Portrait of Dr. Gachet in the late 1990s. In 2001, under financial pressure, Flöttl sold Le Rêve to casino magnate Steve Wynn for an undisclosed sum, estimated at about $60 million. In 2006, Le Rêve was the centerpiece of Wynn's collection, and he had considered naming his Wynn Las Vegas resort after it, but abandoned the idea due to anti-French sentiment in the U.S. in response to France's opposition to the U.S. invasion of Iraq. On 26 October 2006, Wynn told a group of friends—including screenwriter Nora Ephron and her husband Nick Pileggi, broadcaster Barbara Walters, art dealer Serge Sorokko and his wife Tatiana Sorokko, and lawyer David Boies and his wife Mary—that he had agreed to sell Le Rêve to Steve Cohen for $139 million, a price that would have made it the most expensive artwork ever sold at that time. While showing the painting to his friends, Wynn reportedly put his right elbow through the canvas, creating a six-inch tear in the left forearm of the figure. Ephron suggested this was due to Wynn's habit of using wild gestures and his retinitis pigmentosa, which affects peripheral vision. Wynn later stated that the incident convinced him not to sell the painting. After a $90,000 repair, the painting was re-valued at $85 million. Wynn filed a claim with his Lloyd's of London insurers for $54 million, which he claimed represented the perceived loss from the damage, an amount covering most of the original purchase price. When the insurers refused, Wynn sued them in January 2007, and the case was settled out of court in March 2007. Cohen purchased Le Rêve from Wynn in 2013 for $155 million (approximately $134 million in 2006 dollars), a price that, ignoring inflation, was the highest ever paid by a U.S. collector until Kenneth C. Griffin's ~$300 million purchase of Willem de Kooning's Interchange in September 2015.
